had only one possible correct response.  Words coded as incorrect included misspelled words and correctly spelled words that sounded similar to the stimulus word but were different.  Correct homophones, but not filler words, were further coded as a match or mismatch.  A match indicated that the participant wrote the homophone which was presented in the Mandarin tone of the translation of that word.  For example, if the sound “|meɪl|” was presented in the fourth tone, a match response would be “mail,” since the Mandarin translation of “mail” is in the fourth tone. On the other hand, if the participant’s response to that same fourth tone stimulus was “male,” it would be coded as correct but a mismatch, since it does not match the correct translation tone (the translation of “male” is in the second tone).  The participants’ responses were analyzed by computing the number of times each homophone matched its tone, recorded across all items, for each subject.  A match percentage for word choice was computed as the number of matches relative to the number of correct responses.

There were three reaction times recorded in the experiment using Superlab computer software.  The first reaction time was the time for auditory word recognition, the second reaction time was the time for written word production, and the third reaction time was the time for oral production of a simple sentence containing the word. Outliers for each subject were removed if they were 2.5 SD above or below the mean of the reaction times for all the subject’s correct items, whether they were a match or mismatch.  For each subject, reaction times for the experimental stimuli were analyzed and categorized as a match, mismatch, or incorrect, in accordance with the coding described above.

Analyses of variance were performed to examine if there was a difference in how monolinguals and bilinguals matched or mismatched items.  On average, bilinguals chose 11 items correctly, while monolinguals chose 11.65 items correctly out of a total of 12 items.  Of these, bilinguals matched 5.3 items out of 11 correct (percent match = .483, SD = .135), while monolinguals matched 5.95 items out of 11.65 correct (percent match = .511, SD = .151).  See Tables 4 and 5 for word choice matching data.  To test for a difference in word choice matching, an independent samples t-test was performed, which found no significant differences between monolinguals and bilinguals, t(38) = .609, p = .546.

To test differences between bilingual and monolingual performance across reaction times, we ran a 2×3×2 ANOVA examining the interaction between match and mismatch, the three reaction times, and group.  A significant three-way interaction was found, F(1,38) = 6.176, p = 0.017. This indicates that there was a significant reaction time difference between bilinguals’ and monolinguals’ match and mismatch reaction times between the first, second, and third reaction times.  In addition, there was a marginally significant effect of group, with bilinguals performing slower than monolinguals across all three reaction times, F(1,38) = 3.546, p = .067.

In addition, 2×3 ANOVAs were run, one for bilinguals and one for monolinguals, with within-subjects factors of match and mismatch reaction times and the three reaction times to further examine the three-way interaction.  A significant interaction was found in bilinguals between the match and mismatch conditions across reaction times, F(1,19) = 9.589, p = .006.  Follow-up paired t-tests were then run to look at reaction time differences between the match and mismatch conditions for the first, second, and third reaction times.  A graph of bilingual reaction times is shown in Figure 1.  For the first reaction time, bilinguals performed slower for the match (M = 2322.613, SE = 240.889) than for the mismatch condition (M = 2022.074, SE = 163.983), but this did not reach significance, t(19) = 1.600, p = .126 (two-tailed). No significant differences were revealed between match and mismatch conditions for the second reaction time, t(19) = .821, p = .422 (two-tailed).  For the third reaction time, bilinguals performed significantly faster in the match (M = 3361.338, SE = 273.11) than in the mismatch condition (M = 3777.335, SE = 378.93) condition, t(19) = −2.199, p = .040 (two-tailed).
